debate.situation: You are the one who proposes and organizes, and when you stop, the contact goes quiet, though the time you spend together is warm. You haven't said whether you've ever told her this bothers you, or how she reacts when you do ask. What decides this is whether her silence means low interest or simply that she doesn't initiate, and whether you are after reassurance or after a fairer split of the effort.

minds.title: The Honest Requester
minds.concern: Unspoken hurt becomes distance, so name what you observe, what you feel, and one concrete thing you'd like.
minds.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg

minds.title: The Generous Friend
minds.concern: A friendship stays free and noble only when it isn't run like a ledger of who gave what.
minds.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

minds.title: The Maintenance Realist
minds.concern: Friendships weaken without regular contact, and that often reflects habit and logistics more than how much someone cares.
minds.author: Robin Dunbar
minds.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Honest Requester
debate.text: Yes, say something, and keep it small and specific. Going quiet to see what happens teaches you nothing except that you're tired. She can't respond to a pattern nobody has told her is hurting. Describe what you've noticed, say how it feels, and ask for one concrete thing.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Slow down. Plenty of people are warm in person and hopeless at starting things. Friendships fade without contact, and that is often logistics rather than feeling. Before a big talk, ask whether she's a poor planner or a poor friend. What you've told us fits both.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Generous Friend
debate.text: You're both keeping accounts. The moment you count who texts whom, bargaining has crept into something that should be free. Maybe starting things is simply what you give her, and a confrontation turns that gift into a debt. I'd go further than Emerson: some people are natural hosts.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Honest Requester
debate.text: A gift needs to be freely given, and this person is asking whether to speak, which suggests it no longer feels free. Resentment is usually a need nobody said out loud. I'd rather it be named kindly now than harden into a silence she can't read.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Generous Friend
debate.text: Then here is a reading the user can reject. Under the question, they may be after proof that they matter to her, and the texting has become a quiet probe. A friendship built on probes starts to feel like an audit. If that's it, the issue is reassurance, not scheduling.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: A rival reading fits their words equally well. They said always the one making plans, which is about workload. They may simply be tired of being the project manager, with no doubt about her at all. Then you don't ask for love, you ask for a split. Different worry, different sentence.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Honest Requester
debate.text: Good, because my script changes with the answer. If it's doubt: when we don't make plans I feel unsure where we stand, would you sometimes reach out? If it's workload: I've been arranging most of our meetings, could you choose the next one? Neither one accuses her of anything.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Generous Friend
debate.text: I'll concede the script is gentle. But a request can be a demand in polite clothing. Rosenberg himself separates the two by how you take a no. So settle this first: if she shrugs, forgets, or declines, would you still want this friendship? That answer matters more than the wording.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.speaker: The Maintenance Realist
debate.text: Then start with something quieter than a conversation. Hand her a task: your turn to pick the next outing. Stopping altogether is ambiguous, but a clear handover is easy to read. If she steps up, you have your answer without any speech. Contact rhythms are often fixed by small nudges like this.
debate.author: Robin Dunbar
debate.book: Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships
debate.basis: Basis: Robin Dunbar, Friends: Understanding the Power of our Most Important Relationships

debate.speaker: The Honest Requester
debate.text: I'll narrow my claim. Handover first, speech second. But if you've handed her the job clearly, a few weeks pass, and nothing comes back, then saying it plainly is kinder than drifting away resentful. Honesty after a fair trial, not before one.
debate.author: Marshall B. Rosenberg
debate.basis: Basis: Marshall B. Rosenberg, Nonviolent Communication

debate.speaker: The Generous Friend
debate.text: And I'll hold my ground on one point. Some friendships stay lopsided in who moves first and are still deep. If after the handover she mostly just shows up warmly, the real question is whether you can carry that without keeping score. That one belongs to the user, not to a ledger.
debate.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
debate.basis: Basis: Ralph Waldo Emerson, Essays: First Series

debate.clearer: The main insight is that the question may hide two different worries: whether she values you, or whether the effort feels unfair. Those lead to different sentences, and a small, clear handover can test her without any accusation. Still disputed is whether a lopsided friendship needs fixing at all, or whether it can be accepted as it is. One thing to reflect on: when you picture her not replying, does it sting more as being unwanted or as being left with all the work? Only you can say whether either reading sounds like you.
debate.dependsOn:
If the sting is mainly about the workload and she is otherwise warm and engaged → ask her to take a specific turn, because a division of labor is the thing you are missing.
If the sting is mainly doubt about whether she cares → a gentle, honest sentence about how it feels and a request to hear from her sometimes becomes more reasonable, because a task handover won't answer that doubt.
If you could happily keep initiating as long as the evenings stay lovely → doing nothing becomes reasonable, because the friendship may already be giving you what you want.
If you don't know how she responds to a clear handover → try one over a few weeks, then decide whether a plain conversation is needed.
